cards.title: Broaden Media Measurement as You Add Distribution Channels
cards.summary: Measure Meta and YouTube effect on both .com and Amazon via incrementality studies so channel expansion doesn't trigger a false signal to cut spend.
cards.use_when: When Amazon, retail, or marketplace revenue is growing but your .com ROAS is falling and you're considering pulling back on Meta or YouTube spend.
steps: Recognize the failure pattern: as Amazon or retail grows, media measured only against .com looks worse, so you cut spend, and the whole engine stalls.
Run incrementality or geo holdout studies that measure your media's effect on both .com and Amazon revenue, not just .com last-click.
Use the results to set blended efficiency targets across the digital enterprise rather than separate .com-only CAC thresholds.

Expect the split to vary by funnel position (source cites Meta roughly 20% of value landing on Amazon vs 80% on .com, YouTube closer to equal) — treat these as the presenter's portfolio observations, not universal benchmarks.
If a channel pencils only when Amazon effect is included, keep it funded rather than killing it on .com-only reporting.
Run one P&L and one growth plan for .com, Amazon, and retail; siloed budgets and competing P&Ls create false winners and losers.
caveats: Incrementality studies require spend and volume to be directional; sub-scale brands may not get clean reads.
The 20/80 and YouTube parity figures are one advisor's portfolio observations, not established benchmarks.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Channel Playbook by Revenue Stage
cards.summary: Scale your channel mix to your stage: sub-$10M brands stay Meta-first, $10-100M brands expand into Amazon, TikTok Shop, and upper-funnel media.
cards.use_when: When deciding which sales channels and ad platforms to add next, based on current annual revenue.
steps: Under roughly $10M: stay single-channel focused on Meta, with only basic search sprinkling on Google.
$10-100M: expand distribution, starting with Amazon, while broadening media measurement accordingly.
Treat Amazon as demand capture, not demand creation: it captures existing category search volume and does not create net-new category demand.
Build TikTok Shops with an affiliate network and run that channel at roughly neutral margin, treating it as attention and demand creation rather than a direct-response profit center.
Add upper-funnel channels (YouTube, CTV) once broader measurement shows their effect on .com plus Amazon, so they unlock rather than look unprofitable.
Route volume: higher-AOV limited-edition merchandising captures value from true fans, while core SKUs move volume on Amazon — source's observed 2026 pattern, not a rule.
caveats: Stage thresholds (sub-$10M, $10-100M) are the presenter's heuristics, not hard cutoffs; revenue alone doesn't capture category or LTV differences.
Neutral-margin TikTok strategy assumes the attention flywheel lifts other channels — requires measurement to verify for your store.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Amazon Ads and Branded Search as Defensive Tax
cards.summary: Amazon ads and Google branded search defend existing demand rather than create it, and their margin cost rises as category competition increases.
cards.use_when: When deciding how much to budget for Amazon Sponsored Products, Google branded search, or defensive keyword bidding.
steps: Classify these placements as demand capture and defense against competitors on your SERP — not as net-new demand creation.
Budget them as insurance to keep your funnel tight, expecting low incrementality until competition appears on your terms.
Expect margin compression over time in categories with no moat, IP, or defensibility, as rivals bid up your branded terms.
Do not assume turning off Amazon ads kills velocity if upper-funnel channels (e.g., TikTok) are driving demand to Amazon — source cites a brand whose Amazon velocity held after pausing Amazon ads.
Judge these channels on their marginal defensive value against actual competitor encroachment, not standalone ROAS.
Where there is no moat, expect profits to be competed down regardless of tactics — plan product defensibility alongside ad defense.
caveats: The case cited (a fast-growing TikTok brand) is illustrative, not a general rule that Amazon ads never matter.
In commoditized categories competitors may force continued spending even at low incrementality.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Four Quarter Accounting: Break Your P&L into Four Buckets
cards.summary: Review only cost of delivery, CAC, opex, and profit each month to find which bucket eats your profit and where to create leverage.
cards.use_when: When your P&L feels unreadable and you need a simple recurring view to find margin problems in the store's finances.
steps: Ask your accountant to build a monthly view with only four totals: cost of delivery (COGS plus variable fulfillment/payment processing), CAC (marketing), opex (fixed costs), and profit.
Keep CAC as pure variable media dollars only; fixed marketing costs, agencies, and contractors go in opex — but if creative becomes a variable expense, include it in CAC.

Compare against a conceptual even split (25% each); the presenter's reference mix for a strong ecommerce business is roughly 30-40% cost of delivery, 25-30% CAC, 10-15% opex, leaving mid-to-high-teens profit.
Identify which bucket is inflated relative to your model — that's the problem to solve, not a line-item hunt.
Revisit the distribution each month to track where profit is leaking.
caveats: The 25/25/25/25 and 30-40/25-30/10-15 bands are source heuristics, not enforced benchmarks.
CAC definition must stay consistent or the comparison misleads.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Shipping and Cost of Delivery Targets
cards.summary: Track net shipping cost and product cost explicitly, aiming for delivery costs of 30-40% of revenue, because hidden shipping losses quietly kill stores.
cards.use_when: When pricing shipping, evaluating free-shipping thresholds, or auditing fulfillment and 3PL costs.
steps: Break cost of delivery into product cost and shipping; source's reference is roughly 10-20% of revenue for product cost and ~10% for shipping.
Treat shipping above ~20-30% of revenue as a red flag — you're undercharging, or your 3PL or packaging is destroying you.
Track net shipping cost (shipping revenue minus shipping cost) continuously, and use price testing to find willingness to pay for shipping.
Account for value-to-weight ratio: bulky items (e.g., coolers) carry structurally high shipping; small high-AOV items (perfume, jewelry) favor ecommerce.
Watch dimensional thresholds (e.g., packages over ~39 inches on one side) that trigger outsized carrier surcharges.
Keep total cost of delivery in the 30-40% range or accept it will be the biggest problem in the business.
caveats: Ranges depend on product type, LTV, and returns (apparel runs higher due to returns).
Baked-in shipping (drop-ship or fixed-carrier accounts) hides the cost — separate it if possible for clarity.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: CAC Percentage Depends on LTV Model and Stage
cards.summary: High-LTV brands see marketing as a percent of revenue fall over time; low-LTV hard goods must sustain 40-50%+ marketing spend.
cards.use_when: When setting marketing budget as a percentage of revenue, or evaluating whether your CAC is out of line.
steps: Classify your business: high-LTV (repeat purchase, retention value) versus low-LTV (hard goods, one-off purchases without future consumption).
Holding new customer acquisition roughly constant, expect marketing as a percentage of revenue to decline for high-LTV businesses as acquisition cohorts grow and produce repeat revenue.
For low-LTV hard goods, expect marketing to stay closer to 40-50% of revenue because every month requires new acquisition.
Source's median new-customer result on Meta across the portfolio was ~1.7 ROAS (roughly 55-60% cost of acquisition) — treat as a portfolio observation, not a benchmark for your store.
Adjust the target as business stage changes: legacy retailers run ~10% marketing, but that comes from an existing base, not from better ads.
caveats: The 1.7 ROAS and 40-50% figures are the presenter's data across his portfolio, not a universal standard.
Falling marketing percentage requires a stable acquisition engine and real retention; if retention is weak, the model breaks.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Aged Inventory Tiers and Liquidation Funnels
cards.summary: Tier inventory A-D, and liquidate slow stock through unlisted funnels with lower efficiency targets rather than letting cash decay on shelves.
cards.use_when: When you have aging SKUs sitting in the warehouse and need to decide whether to discount, liquidate, or hold.
steps: Tier inventory A, B, C, D by days outstanding; aim for days-of-inventory remaining to roughly match production lead time so a PO placed today arrives just as you run out (just-in-time ideal).
When sales velocity drops and you're stuck with far more inventory than production time (e.g., 1,000 days outstanding), treat it as a cash flow problem, not a margin problem.
Liquidate non-moving stock always — it decays in value, and sophisticated buyers won't assign balance-sheet retail value to 2-year-old stock.

Build liquidation funnels: create an unlisted PDP, run ads to it, exclude existing customers, and accept lower efficiency (e.g., ~1.0 or 0.8 ROS versus a 2:1 target on good inventory) or discount deeply.
Build relationships with third-party liquidators as a standing capability for large inventory positions.
Alternatively, sell to your large customer list with a discount and a narrative where it won't damage the brand.
caveats: Liquidating harms the P&L and reported margin — that's accepted in exchange for cash.
Holding aged inventory to prop up asset ratios overstates its true value.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Sync Demand Creation with Inventory Position
cards.summary: Match ad spend to days-of-inventory on your best SKUs: raise efficiency expectations or pause when you're about to sell through, so you maximize marginal value per batch.
cards.use_when: When your media buyer is pushing your best sellers and you want to avoid stockouts or waste marginal margin.
steps: Hold a weekly inventory meeting with your media buyer covering days of inventory outstanding on top SKUs and where ads are currently pointing.
If a top SKU has only ~30 days of stock versus ~80 days to reorder, either raise the efficiency (ROAS) expectation to capture maximum marginal value on that batch, or turn ads off entirely.
Do not pay high CAC to move inventory about to go out of stock — that minimizes marginal capture on the batch and wastes spend.
Every PO placed should aim to maximize the marginal value of that inventory batch, not just push total volume.
Shift spend to other SKUs, and ensure demand planning and demand creation are in sync rather than run by disconnected teams.
caveats: Without inventory visibility, media buyers will optimize the wrong way by default.
Requires discipline to accept lower spend when demand planning and ad throughput are misaligned.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Vendor Terms and Cost-of-Capital Arbitrage
cards.summary: Negotiate net terms using each partner's cost of capital and cash needs — pay more margin for longer terms, or take on consignment over dropshipping and full inventory ownership.
cards.use_when: When negotiating supplier, agency, or software contracts and choosing between dropshipping, buying inventory, or consignment.
steps: Understand each counterpart's cost of capital and cash cycle; suppliers with cheaper capital (e.g., subsidized manufacturing) may accept a small price increase in exchange for longer net terms.
Aim for payment terms that extend past your production and sell-through timeline so your customer's money pays the manufacturer — a negative cash conversion cycle.
Recognize the trade matrix: some vendors value margin, some want committed/long-term dollars, some need cash flow — offer the thing they value for the term you want.
Target consignment as the ideal middle: a supplier holds inventory on your behalf and you pay when you sell — you get dropshipping's cash benefit plus inventory pricing.
Build trust with suppliers over time; consignment and long terms are granted on demonstrated reliability, not negotiation alone.
caveats: Consignment and extended terms require relationships built on trust and track record.
Extreme structures (e.g., an in-house lender floated to a vendor) require scale and leverage most brands don't have.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Turn Liquidation and Discount Levers into Cash for New Bets
cards.summary: Whatever the liquidation method, the objective is to convert dead stock to cash fast and make a new bet — never pay to store inventory with no sell plan.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to hold, discount, or dump inventory that has no active selling plan.
steps: Inventory with no ads, emails, or promotion plan is decaying cash — retrieve it and turn it back into cash.

Choose the liquidation method based on brand risk and speed: unlisted ad funnels (fast, hidden from customers), discount to your list with a narrative (faster but brand-visible), or bulk liquidation (fastest, lowest price).
Accept a lower efficiency target on liquidation funnels than on your core inventory to accelerate cash recovery.
Reinvest recovered cash into new inventory bets — the goal is optionality and cash flow, not idle balance-sheet assets.
When considering retail or new channels as outlets, confirm the sale reaches genuinely new buyers rather than cannibalizing existing channels.
caveats: Liquidation reduces P&L margin and blended contribution — that's the tradeoff.
Cannibalization risk is real: opening a store or retailer in a region where you already have strong direct distribution may just shift the same customers.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Menu of Growth Channels Beyond Meta and Amazon
cards.summary: Add channels per their role: AppLovin and gaming ad networks as incremental new-customer sources, CTV tied to moments where broad distribution can capture the value.
cards.use_when: When selecting the next paid platform to test after Meta and Google.
steps: Layer AppLovin (mobile gaming ad network) where you need forced-view, incremental new customers; source reports 3-5% share of wallet for big spenders and incrementality tests showing 100%+ incremental (matching or exceeding platform-reported results) — treat as his observation, not a promise.
Add YouTube and CTV once broad distribution (Amazon, retail) exists to capture value from non-click viewership.
If you run CTV without broad distribution (e.g., .com exclusive), expect it to be hard to pencil on .com alone — the value is realized wherever the customer shops.
Align CTV with cultural peaks (e.g., the Olympics, seasonal moments) to amplify existing demand spikes rather than spread always-on.
Treat podcast, Pinterest, Snapchat, and X as category-specific bets; source has not seen them reliably unlock scale across a large portfolio.
Require incrementality measurement before or during any new channel test to decide if value is real.
caveats: AppLovin incrementality and share numbers are the presenter's observations; verify your own lift.
CTV's value depends on having Amazon/retail presence; without it, measurement makes CTV look unprofitable.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: CTV as a Complement to Broad Distribution and Moments
cards.summary: Deploy CTV when you have multiple places for viewers to buy, and align airtime with cultural peaks to amplify demand rather than run it standalone.
cards.use_when: When planning a CTV campaign and deciding whether your channel mix can support it.
steps: Confirm prerequisites: .com + Amazon + retail presence ensures non-click viewers can convert somewhere.
Coordinate CTV flighting with recognizable moments (holidays, sports events) so you're attaching to demand spikes rather than fighting for baseline attention.

Buy via publishers/networks that reach real audiences; source cites Comcast's Universal Ads as one access point with no fees and Meta-like workflow — verify current interface and fees before committing.
Push for measurement: source notes at least one CTV provider requires incrementality testing as a condition — adopt that standard for your own tests.
Do not run CTV as an isolated .com-only performance channel; expect measurement to look weak until broad distribution and blended measurement are in place.
caveats: CTV is hard to pencil on .com exclusively; results depend on the rest of the channel mix.
Platform access and pricing change — verify current offerings before budgeting.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Four Quarter Accounting vs Cash Flow: Tradeoffs Are Purposeful
cards.summary: Profitability and cash flow are different games — knowingly sacrifice gross margin or P&L efficiency when it accelerates cash and optionality.
cards.use_when: When weighing a decision that hurts P&L margin but improves cash position, such as liquidation, longer-term vendor deals, or consignment.
steps: Keep the two views distinct: four quarter accounting analyzes the P&L; cash flow and the balance sheet are managed separately and can call for opposing moves.
Prioritize growing the bank account — it creates optionality, especially when M&A and funding are constrained.
Accept tactics that worsen the P&L (liquidation margins, discounting, extended supplier terms) when they convert dead stock or float into usable cash.
Reinvest recovered cash into new inventory bets or growth rather than holding it in depreciating assets.
Review both views regularly so tradeoffs are deliberate rather than accidental.
caveats: Repeated P&L erosion without cash conversion isn't strategy — the tradeoff must produce usable cash.
Overstating balance-sheet inventory to satisfy asset ratios obscures the cash reality.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Constraint as a Growth Superpower
cards.summary: A hard CAC/ROAS ceiling forces creative problem-solving — storytelling, creative, channel expansion, product development — instead of buying growth with efficiency.
cards.use_when: When your media team keeps asking to raise the CAC ceiling or lower ROAS targets to hit growth goals.
steps: Set a firm ceiling on CAC/ROAS based on your unit economics and payback period; do not allow it to move.
When asked to raise it, redirect the team to solve differently: better creative, storytelling peaks, new channels, influencer programs, product development.

Use the source's lesson from 2021: analysis across a portfolio found ~60% of media dollars never repaid — illustrating what happens when constraint is absent (presented as one analysis, not a universal rate).
Set the expectation explicitly to your media buyer or team: 'this is the cap, don't come back with a request to raise it.'
Expect constraint to unlock energy that improves product and distribution, not just ad tactics.
Give creative people a bounded box rather than a blank page — constraints unlock better creative output.
caveats: The 60% figure is a single 2021 portfolio analysis, not an industry benchmark.
Constraint needs accurate CAC and LTV/ payback numbers behind it — otherwise it's arbitrary.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Ecommerce Is a Low-Opex Model — Track Revenue per Employee
cards.summary: Winning ecommerce runs a lean fixed cost base (~10-15% opex benchmark), and your fixed dollars of opex should fall year over year even as revenue grows.
cards.use_when: When auditing team size, software costs, and overhead, or planning AI/tooling investments to raise output per person.
steps: Target opex in the ballpark of 10-15% of revenue for a strong ecommerce business; source has watched the standard slide from 25% down over time.
Aim for fixed opex dollars to decline every year even when revenue doubles — source argues this is non-negotiable in the current environment.
Deploy AI and tooling to raise output per person (source cites stores reaching $1M-$5M revenue per employee).
At 15%+ opex, prioritize leverage over headcount; treat labor as the first place to look for compression, given marketing demand on the P&L.
Recognize that whoever can spend more to acquire a customer wins competitive sets — cost discipline protects your acquisition ceiling.
caveats: Extremely low opex can strain quality and retention; source's argument assumes AI/tooling can replace the lost capacity.
The 10-15% and revenue-per-employee figures are the presenter's observations, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Don't Let .com Efficiency Reports Choke the Whole-Enterprise Engine
cards.summary: When media drives all channels but is measured only on .com, declining .com efficiency signals a pullback that stalls growth of the entire business.
cards.use_when: When reviewing .com performance and feeling pressure to cut spend on Meta/YouTube because only .com attribution looks soft.
steps: Before cutting spend, ask where the demand is landing — Amazon, retail, marketplaces may be capturing value your reporting ignores.
Compare: if Amazon and retail are growing while .com efficiency 'declines,' the problem is measurement, not the ads.
Run holdouts or incrementality studies to see total business lift before pulling budget.
Ensure finance, media, and operations report one blended view of contribution margin, not separate channel P&Ls competing against each other.
Treat retail endcap and store placements partly as marketing (awareness in new geographies) — but verify incrementality before assuming retail expands demand.
Be cautious about promises that retail or marketplace launches will be net-new; if the same customers shift channels, value doesn't grow.
caveats: Retail channel value varies: a Nordstrom-style launch that sits on your brand terms may siphon demand without net-new customers.
Blended measurement requires methodology discipline; sloppy attribution can just as easily hide real unprofitability.
